 A real session: the file panel, a shell following a deploy log, and the assistant reading the same terminal. 
 

Motty is a desktop SSH client. The terminal, the SFTP panel, port forwards,
remote desktops and an AI assistant share one window, so a session does not
need a second app for files or a browser tab for a screen.

The full documentation lives at ; this file covers
the project, the packages and how to build it.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 Why Motty?

 
 
 
 Hosts stay organised. Groups, tags, colours and icons, importable from
 OpenSSH config, PuTTY, MobaXterm and five more. Passwords go to an
 AES-256-GCM vault; the key lives in the system secret store. 
 
 
 A session you can watch. Split the pane, then read the host's
 CPU, memory, disk and network beside the shell that is using them. 
 
 
 
 
 Screens too, when you need them. VNC and RDP connect, and both can
 ride an SSH host when the server only listens on its own loopback. 
 
 
 Tunnels you can see. Local, remote, SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT
 rules bind to loopback only, are saved, and start when you say so. A tunnel
 stops with the SSH tab that owns it. 
 
 
 

 Keyboard first. Tabs, splits, SFTP, forwarding and the assistant are
commands in the palette; the mouse is optional. Mosh when the network
moves: an SSH host can carry its terminal over Mosh, keeping the session
through Wi-Fi, hotspot and VPN changes and drawing slow-link typing before the
echo; docs/mosh.md lists what such a session does not carry.
 Honest about limits: 
docs/remote-desktop.md lists what the VNC and RDP
implementations do not do, and the release notes say which platforms were
tested on real hardware. Nothing phones home: no analytics, and the update
check is off by default and asks GitHub Releases when you turn it on.

 Install

Download the package for your platform from the
releases page:

 Platform Packages 
 --- --- 
 macOS (arm64, amd64) .dmg , .zip 
 Windows (amd64, arm64) .exe installer, portable .zip (data kept in motty-data beside motty.exe ) 
 Linux (amd64, arm64) .deb , .tar.gz 

Windows packages require Windows 10 or Windows Server 2016 or later.

macOS builds are signed and notarized when the release has the credentials.
Windows builds are signed when a certificate is configured. Linux packages are
not signed. AUR and .AppImage are not available yet.

Through a package manager:

 

If Homebrew asks you to trust the tap first, run brew trust t8y2/tap once.

 

The cask installs the notarized disk image and is marked as self-updating, so an
installed copy updates itself. A manually unpacked Windows portable ZIP can
update itself when a signed release is available; it keeps motty-data intact.
Older portable builds need one manual ZIP replacement before this is available.
Scoop installs the portable copy but manages its version directories: its
 motty-data folder is persisted across versions and scoop update motty is how
it updates.

 Quick start

1. Open Hosts and choose New host .
2. Enter a name, address and account name.
3. Pick authentication: the running agent, a private-key file or the password.
4. Connect and compare the host-key fingerprint with the server. Trust it once or
 save it.
5. The tab opens on the login shell. A server that asks for a one-time code gets
 the extra field automatically.

The command palette is Command+Shift+P on macOS and Control+Shift+P 
elsewhere. Default shortcuts use Command on macOS and Control on Windows/Linux;
all of them are configurable.

 Action macOS Windows / Linux 
 --- --- --- 
 Command palette Command+Shift+P Control+Shift+P 
 Find in terminal Command+F Control+F 
 Command history Command+Shift+H Control+Shift+H 
 File panel Command+Shift+S Control+Shift+S 
 New window Command+Shift+N Control+Shift+N 

On Windows, choose the local shell from the dropdown in Settings → Terminal
→ Local shell , below Inline suggestions . Motty detects installed shells
such as PowerShell, CMD and Git Bash from PATH and common installation folders,
and lists each installed WSL distribution as its own entry. A tab or side-bar
row shows the shell's own mark, and a distribution shows its logo. The file
panel opens inside a WSL terminal's distribution, through the distribution's
 \\wsl.localhost share, and follows the folder the shell reports; the resource
monitor samples the distribution itself. Choose the distribution here, rather
than typing wsl into PowerShell: only a shell Motty starts itself can report
its folder. The choice stays on this computer and applies to new or reconnected
local terminals.

features.title: Features
features.html:
The terminal

Real PTY sessions, 256-colour and true-colour output, the alternate screen, 5,000 lines of scrollback, wide and combining characters, mouse reporting, input methods and window resizing that follows the pty. Synchronized updates (DECSET 2026) keep a full-screen redraw atomic, the kitty keyboard protocol reports presses, releases and unambiguous Escape/Alt keys, and Windows local shells can use win32-input-mode. Font ligatures are shaped inside the fixed-pitch grid. Tabs can be reordered, split horizontally or vertically, moved between windows and restored without reconnecting.

Choose Settings > General > Tab orientation for horizontal tabs or a vertical list in the left sidebar. In terminal workspaces, keep the vertical list expanded or let it collapse to an icon rail that expands on hover without resizing the terminal. These layout preferences stay on this device.

Group vertical tabs is a separate General setting, off by default. When enabled, multiple tabs for the same connection target appear under a collapsible server heading; a single connection stays a standalone tab. Different accounts, protocols, ports or local shell environments, and split tabs spanning multiple servers, stay separate. Grouping only changes the vertical list: it never merges or disconnects sessions, and turning it off or returning to horizontal mode restores the original order.

Window and terminal toolbar icons can be dragged to the top, either side's upper or lower group, or either end of the bottom bar. A drop commits on release; Escape or dropping outside a dock keeps the layout unchanged. Right-click an icon to move or hide it, customize the toolbar, or restore its default layout. Settings > General also controls visibility, order and position. Placements stay on this device, and terminal actions follow the active split. The SFTP toolbar keeps its separate visibility and ordering settings.

Settings > General > Terminal toolbar > Customize offers small, medium and large sizes for both side rails and the bottom bar, including relocated window actions. The choice stays on this device; top-bar icons keep their standard size. Connection colors remain on tabs and host markers, while terminal, file and monitor headers use neutral backgrounds.

Search the retained history, open HTTP/HTTPS and OSC 8 links, render Kitty/iTerm2/SIXEL images, send snippets, broadcast input across a split tab, or record a session explicitly. The terminal ships with more than two hundred colour schemes, keyword highlighting and optional inline command suggestions. Settings keeps a short set of quick picks and opens the rest in a left-hand drawer; X resources files in the data folder's schemes directory join the list.

Hosts and authentication

Host keys are verified against Motty's own known_hosts before credentials are sent. Authentication covers agent keys, identity files, OpenSSH user certificates (the -cert.pub companion of a key file is picked up the way OpenSSH pairs them), PuTTY .ppk files (versions 2 and 3, Argon2id included), passwords and keyboard-interactive rounds. A round that asks several questions — for example a password and a one-time code from the same PAM stack — is shown as one dialog with one field per question. Hosts presenting a certificate connect without a prompt once their CA is on file as @cert-authority, and an unknown certificate is asked about with its fingerprint, like any unknown key. A host can also forward the local ssh-agent to its shells, per host and off by default.

Hardware security keys (sk-ssh-ed25519, sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256) authenticate through OpenSSH's agent and ssh-sk-helper. For a connection that uses one, Motty starts a short-lived agent, loads the key with ssh-add, and shows its PIN or passphrase prompt in the window; the key list marks it as a security key. See security keys for the requirements and limits.

Hosts can be grouped, tagged, searched and imported from OpenSSH config, PuTTY, Xshell, MobaXterm, WindTerm, Electerm, Netcatty or SecureCRT. TOTP/HOTP seeds can be stored in the vault and filled automatically. Saved passwords and key passphrases go into an AES-256-GCM vault, kept under the host they belong to; the vault key lives in the system secret store, or in a key file beside the vault where there is none (and in a portable copy). Electerm and Netcatty imports can save readable SSH passwords with explicit consent; re-import only fills missing passwords. SecureCRT stores its saved passwords encrypted, so its import carries connections only.

OpenSSH config import and sync retain per-host ServerAliveInterval, ServerAliveCountMax, IdentitiesOnly and configured identity files. An explicit zero interval disables keepalive for that host; restricted identities still use matching keys from the SSH agent, without offering unrelated agent keys. A host that uses automatic authentication can set the same restriction in the host editor's Advanced section: the agent then offers only the keys matching the configured identities, so a large agent key set cannot spend the server's authentication budget before the local keys are tried.

Files

SFTP browsing with multi-select, recursive upload/download, copy and paste between the local and server sides, a bounded transfer queue, resume, cancel/retry, rename, delete, permissions and bookmarks. Replacing a file stages a partial copy, verifies resumed prefixes and renames atomically only after a complete synced copy. The previous file stays intact on failure.

A native editor opens UTF-8 files up to 1 MiB, hashes the remote file before and after staging, and preserves permissions. Servers without SFTP can use the built-in SCP fallback. It edits code in a fixed-pitch grid with line numbers, syntax colors, bracket matching, soft wrap, auto-indent that follows the file's own tabs or spaces, paired brackets and quotes, Tab/Shift+Tab block indent, line comment toggling (Cmd/Ctrl+/), line move/copy/delete (Alt+Up/Down, Shift+Alt+Up/Down, Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+K), find and replace (Cmd/Ctrl+F, Ctrl+H) with case, whole-word and regular-expression options, and go to line (Ctrl+G).

For files that the SSH account can read but cannot change (such as root-owned configuration), switch on the sudo toggle beside the remote pane title (or choose Use sudo for remote files in the file context menu) and confirm the password. The same toggle stays selected while sudo is active; click it again to return to normal mode. This switches the current file browser, its transfers and open documents to a privileged SFTP server. Remote tools and the terminal's resource monitor have a separate sudo control, while each dashboard host requires its own confirmation. Sudo is off by default, never elevates the terminal, and passwords are held only for the connection, not saved. The remote host needs sudo and an OpenSSH sftp-server executable; Windows servers and SCP-only servers cannot use privileged SFTP. Server sudo policies may deny the required shell command.

The panel's more menu can hand the folder it shows to VS Code or Zed through the editor's own URL scheme. Pick the editor under Settings > Files, which lists the editors installed on this computer; until one is picked the menu item stays hidden. A server is opened under the alias your SSH config gives that very host (same address, user and port), or as user@host; a host reached through a jump host that only Motty keeps is refused, because the editor's own ssh would not use it.

The attached file panel can follow the SSH terminal's folder automatically for Bash and Zsh. Settings > Files also offers a separate, default-off switch for the terminal to follow file navigation at a ready, empty prompt. See folder synchronization for safety and startup compatibility details.

Forwarding and jump chains

Local, remote, SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT rules are loopback-only, persisted and started explicitly. Tunnels stop with the SSH tab that owns them. Jump routes verify and authenticate every hop independently. A global outbound SOCKS5/HTTP proxy can carry the initial connection; each saved network host can inherit it, force a direct connection, use its own SOCKS5/HTTP proxy, or connect through a proxy command such as cloudflared access ssh (OpenSSH's ProxyCommand). X11 forwarding validates a per-session fake cookie before replacing it with the local Xauthority cookie.
